utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. General, you may be seated. For the record, I note that Mr. Krstic, who has been subpoenaed by the Chamber to testify in this case and his counsel, Mr. Visnjic, are present in this courtroom. General Krstic, during the hearing of 21st of March, 2013, the Chamber denied your request for reconsideration of its oral ruling of 13th of March, in which you were ultimately ordered to testify in this case today. I instructed the Registry to communicate this ruling to you and your counsel and I take it you have been duly notified, Mr. Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, the Chamber is going to ask you one last time whether you are willing to testify today, but before it does so I wish to make sure once more that you fully understand the potential consequences resulting from your refusal to comply with the Chamber's order. Mr. Krstic, are you aware of such consequences and has your counsel fully explained to you about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm aware of all the consequences and also my counsel has explained fully what the consequences may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krstic, I will now ask you one last time if you maintain your refusal to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For reasons that you are aware of, I have not changed my position and I will not testify in these proceedings. I simply cannot do anything that would go against my health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, the Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, before your decision may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record and for the benefit of the witness and his counsel, I would like to say that I understand his position but I have three questions that I can put only to this witness and nobody else: Did the two of us plan to kill the prisoners? Was I informed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there's no point you repeat your position. It does not mean you are withdrawing your motion to subpoena the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will not entertain your submission at this moment, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Krstic, the Chamber will proceed to issue an order in lieu of indictment in due course and will schedule a hearing date for an initial appearance at which you will be asked to enter into a plea of guilty or not guilty. You may be excused, General. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So next witness is Mr. Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Mr. President. We'll need a little time to regroup and I think Mr. Robinson has to come in so this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we break for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe ten would be a little better I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please. Mr. Vucurevic, do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucurevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Vucurevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any questions from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucurevic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must ask you, like all the other witnesses who speak Serbian, that you and I should make pauses between questions and answers, and I would also like to ask you to articulate in order to make it possible for the interpreters to interpret everything and for the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure I understand what the accused is referring to. utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC

utterances.text: But do you have a hard copy in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I think that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Vucurevic, do you not see your document -- your statement in your language on the left part of your monitor? Do you not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in my mother tongue -- oh, I'm sorry, sorry, sorry. Can you please turn the volume on a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me well now, Mr. Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear you well. Yes, this is in my mother tongue and I'm reading it and understanding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this statement and have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I confirm what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, completely it reflects what I said. I'm talking about what you can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put today live the same questions that were asked of you at that time, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is only one truth and all I can do is to repeat the truth.

utterances.text: Does that mean that you would provide basically exactly the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

In addition, I believe this may have been noted in Mr. Robinson's e-mail or at least alluded to, but 1D -- oppose 1D07093 contains in part a previously admitted exhibit, which is found at D00471, so one way or another that logistical issue needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1D --

utterances.text: Is it being tendered at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are certain documents about which there is no English translations. For example, do we have English translation for 1D7096?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to check my e-court, but I believe that all of these have been translated but I'll check.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't of sufficient assistance to the Court. I had previously noted the existence of two -- at least two documents for which there was no English translation. I didn't find them, but I don't have my list with me and that's why I didn't allude to them when the Court asked and I apologise for that, but it appears the Court is well-informed on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do have the English translation in our e-court, but apparently it hasn't made its way to the rest of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Among the associated exhibits tendered, we'll not admit two intercepted conversations referred to by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I play them for the purpose of authenticating the voices of the participants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to consult with Mr. Robinson how to proceed on your part with respect to those intercepts. There are certain documents the Chamber may raise some concerns, but for the sake of time the -- all the other associated exhibits will be admitted and be given numbers in due course. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read brief summary of Mr. Bozidar Vucurevic's statement in English. [In English] Bozidar Vucurevic was born on 14th of October, 1936, in Zubci near Trebinje. In 1990 he was elected as a member of the Main Board of the SDS, established in response to the formation of the HDZ and SDA. In this capacity, Bozidar Vucurevic did his utmost to ensure that the minority people in the region were not mistreated. His action in protecting the non-Serbian population and preventing ethnic clashes were praised by both Momcilo Krajisnik and Dr. Radovan Karadzic. In 1992 Mr. Bozidar Vucurevic became president of the Crisis Staff of the Trebinje municipality, where he previously was president of the municipality, and a Crisis Staff was formed that at least some kind of government would be operational once clashes broke out with the exclusive purpose of protecting the civilian population. Each municipality functioned as a separate unit. There were no instructions from the party leaderships whatsoever. Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik could not have influenced the work of the Crisis Staff even if they had wished to. The military leadership frequently ignored Dr. Karadzic's directives. Herzegovina in particular, given the separation in both territory and communications, operated quite independently. Dr. Karadzic did ensure a clear directive that the civilian population must not be maltreated and that it was necessary to abide by provisions of international humanitarian law. In 1991 the mobilisation of the JNA was carried out by the newly formed Trebinje military department, an organ comprised of two Muslims and a Croat and none of the Serbs. Following this, when Muslims asked to leave the JNA or the municipality of Trebinje all together, this request was granted provided they provided a certificate showing that they had returned their weapons and equipment. No conditions were required for civilians. There was no forcible transfer of Muslims from Trebinje. Only SDA party forced individuals to leave with the aim of provoking a conflict between Muslims and Serbs. Bozidar Vucurevic nonetheless gave the order to secure the civilian convoy moving out of Trebinje in order to help those people. Dr. Karadzic and Bozidar Vucurevic were concerned that all people in the area were treated equally regardless of their ethnicity. Bozidar Vucurevic often had meetings with Muslim authorities in an attempt to develop an atmosphere of tolerance and reconciliation. Dr. Karadzic often said in private conversations between the two that clashes needed to be prevented especially where Serbs were in the majority so that minority population would not feel threatened. He also urged that the leadership in the municipalities be composed of people who were honest and levelheaded who did not contribute to the rise of tensions between the people. In late 1992 an armed paramilitary group took some areas of Trebinje by force. Bozidar Vucurevic wrote an order to remove the group by force if necessary, after which he was personally threatened. The group eventually left the area in response to Bozidar Vucurevic's actions. The authorities in the municipality generally used all the available means to prevent crime, regardless of the perpetrators or the injured parties. [Interpretation] Now, this was a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask Mr. Vucurevic to listen to an intercept and then to identify the collocutors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please play 1D05685 from 0:20 to 2 minutes 50.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we do not have the transcript of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it seems that it would be impossible for the Chamber to hear the transcript unless it was provided to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a translation, so could we please have it on the screens even though we are going to listen only to the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's possible, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it translated. Is there a way to see it or to have it sent to the booth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have a print-out there's no difficulty on the part of the Registry to provide it [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I understand that either Mr. Doraiswamy or Mr. Reid can print it out immediately if that's the preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the Defence is going to play two intercepts I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we also have 1D05684. We also wanted the witness to identify the collocutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I will leave it to the parties, in particular to the Defence, to play it and to tender the document. Mr. Robinson, has the Chamber ever admitted intercept when witness confirms the voice of one of the interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe in those cases you've always admitted -- marked them for identification subject to the testimony of the intercept operator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Or the interlocutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have -- we admitted them in full?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. So these two we would ask you to mark them for identification and we will try to bring the intercept operators to include them when we have them testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If that is the case, I take it that the Prosecution would have no objection to marking them for identification, as part of associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I think that was done previously and in any event I think it would make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that would resolve everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic actually wanted to play these two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber also would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we start then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need to find the reference in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We stop there. We play again. The interpreters want to know the reference, what part of the transcript you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of page 1, the fourth intervention from the bottom in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was offered to the interpreters is the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fourth from the bottom in the English version too on page 1. The first conversation of the 24th of May between Radovan Karadzic and an unidentified male person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unknown male person: I didn't know that it was such a meeting. I was just looking ... and Saso here ... "Radovan Karadzic: Who ... well ... these Muslims, they were panicking so we ... them ... "Unknown male person: Where were they from? "Radovan Karadzic: Ah ... they were ... I don't know whether they were from Ljubinje and Stolac but there were some from ... Gacko, Bileca, and Trebinje. "Unknown male person: Mm-hmm. "Radovan Karadzic: Go on, please. Everyone needs to tell them over there that the Serbs have nothing against them, that the Serbs ... only attitude towards Ustashas ... go on ... "Unknown male person: ... they said on the radio at four and I spoke for two and a half minutes exactly about that. He asked me about the political situation. I told Vatric that I was terribly sorry that they once again managed to direct ... to throw a bone of contention between the Serbs and the Muslims even though there is no ... even though everyone can see that these are, in fact, conflict between the Serbs and the Croats. "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. "Unknown male person: They have no reason ... it's the Muslim Bosniak Organisation that's pushing ... "Radovan Karadzic: The MBO is pushing, huh? "Unknown male person: Yes, only the MBO. There was a headline in the "Oslobodjenje" today that said, 'Three more trucks' ... and such ugly, stupid things. Were it not ... "Radovan Karadzic: Yes. "Unknown male person: They won't broadcast that. We had a meeting here with their hosts and talked about trust and that is the worst-case scenario. We'll rely on each other ... there's no such news on the ... "Radovan Karadzic: All right, all right. Please call Bozo and tell him the same so that ... he can call them immediately tonight or tomorrow. Nikola is going to Bileca tomorrow afternoon too ... "Unknown male person: Mm-hmm. "Radovan Karadzic: He should call them, sit down with them, and tell them not to worry because they don't have ... just tell us who's threatening you and we'll fucking sort them out ... "Unknown male person: Yes, yes. "Radovan Karadzic: Nobody may threaten them. They must pay a fine and they must know that neighbours or neighbourly arguments will not resolve the Yugoslav crisis ... "Unknown male person: Mm-hmm. "Radovan Karadzic: It will be resolved by political means. We had discussions with Izetbegovic and Kljuic today as well. The first thing we agreed on is that we don't want a civil war. "Unknown male person: Mm-hmm. "Radovan Karadzic: And we ... we don't want a civil war, we don't want a civil war in Bosnia. "Unknown male person: Yes, yes. "Radovan Karadzic: And all the other options can be considered and we ... we'll agree about every option, but we don't want a civil war. "Unknown male person: Yes, yes ... "Radovan Karadzic: And the neighbours need to know that their blood will not resolve anything but just makes -- make matters worse, more complicated. "Unknown male person: Yes, yes, yes. "Radovan Karadzic: Therefore, err ...Danilo, Danilo/talking to someone in the room/I keep forgetting something. Err, therefore, please make sure they feel fine... "Unknown male person: Excellent ... "Radovan Karadzic: It's very important, that they ... "Unknown male person: ... initiate a meeting, if not tomorrow then the day after with this ... again with this man here ... "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes ... "Unknown male person: I'll see that I personally ... if I can, this ... "Radovan Karadzic: Very well. "Unknown male person: To help them and to change their mind about ... "Radovan Karadzic: Go on, please and ... and ... "Unknown male person: ... and this on the news ... looking at that guard in Zagreb. "Radovan Karadzic: What happened with the guard in Zagreb? "Unknown male person: It was a troop review. Tudjman was reviewing the troops and TV Belgrade broadcast the whole thing, how there was the 1st Brigade, 2nd, 3rd, they, they ... the war flags ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, did you recognise the interlocutor, the person who talked to me in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I carefully listened to it, I recognised both participants in the conversation. You are on one end of the line, Mr. President, and on the other there is Dusan Kozic who was from Ljubinje. He was a deputy in the People's Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on in the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the contents of this intercept. Is the topic familiar to you and how? Tell us something about the topic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: May I? Yes, I am familiar with it. That conversation was reflected, such policies, such positions that could be heard from you as of the moment the SDS was established and until the end of the war. There was always discussion about avoiding clashes, initiating talks, and if we must go our separate ways, then that it should be done in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we next listen to 1D05684 now from the third minute to 4 minutes and 20, and I'll tell you what page that is in the English transcript. Actually, we'll start with 1 minute, 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have time reference on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 3 in the English towards the bottom, Mulic -- Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan Karadzic: Tell me ... "Vlado Kovacevic: Well, it's about the rally and Delalic. "Radovan Karadzic: Who is Delalic? "Kovacevic: Delalic is the proposed candidate for the SUP commander. "Karadzic: Oh, I see. "Kovacevic: For the militia commander. "Karadzic: The militia commander. "Kovacevic: Yes, you know the story very well recently we have ... regarding this candidate ... "Karadzic: Yes. "Kovacevic: ... but the tensions are higher up. It looks they could rise even more and we are not sure how it would end up. "Karadzic: Because of Delalic? "Kovacevic: Yes. "Karadzic: I've just been at the meeting with the Muslims from eastern Herzegovina and Nikola Koljevic and Alija Izetbegovic. They spent two hours together. "Kovacevic: Yes. "Karadzic: I got in for 15 to 20 minutes and talked to them. They are afraid and say that you haven't given them anything in the municipality there. "Kovacevic: We haven't? Well, the negotiations between our parties are ongoing and I don't think they have a right to say so. "Karadzic: Yes, yes. "Kovacevic: ... it means they got what they were supposed to get, but they should also know it can't be as it used to be. Karadzic: Yes, please. See it with them and call Zepinic regarding that ... tell them not to be worried because Serbs will not do anything. Serbs are careful only with the Ustasha. Tell them that. "Kovacevic: Of course, we are doing that ... " Karadzic: Please organise a meeting with the SDA tonight. Tell them not to be worried and we guarantee that nothing will happen to the Muslims in eastern Herzegovina. Our only concern is the Ustashas. But you can tell them that we guarantee nothing will happen to them. Do that tonight. "Kovacevic: Okay. We planned to do that tomorrow morning. "Karadzic: Okay. Anyone -- announce it tonight and meet tomorrow morning and issue some kind of joint statement, that eastern Herzegovina - you can mention Gacko specifically - will be peaceful, that all the issues be solved democratically, and that there is no danger of a conflict. This is very important to convince Muslims that we have nothing against them. "Kovacevic: Okay. Thanks. Would you mind talking to the mayor for a second? "Karadzic: No. "Kovacevic: Have a nice day! "Karadzic: You too."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting from 4 minutes, 20 seconds and onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Karadzic: Fine, thanks God. A lot of work but I can manage ... "Mandic: Your health? Karadzic: It's good. Thanks God ... "Mandic: So it's okay. What's up? "Karadzic: Well, I've just talked to the Muslims from eastern Herzegovina. They are panicking and talking about Chetniks. I told them that those Nemanjic badges are not Chetnik cockades. You should explain to them that those are not Chetnik cockades and please meet them and convince them that the Muslims are not endangered. "Mandic: Well, we've had meetings between the parties over there. "Karadzic: Okay. But they have been there, some people from Gacko too. Tonight they complained of not getting any position in the government. I told them that the Muslims in Gacko should get the same as Serbs in Gorazde. "Mandic: They got more than the Serbs in Gorazde. "Karadzic: So tell them that. Make it clear so they wouldn't be able to say that they got less. "Mandic: Well, it's their policy. "Karadzic: I know. But still make this clear for them somehow and publicise it together. Say there is no danger for them whatsoever. "Mandic: Okay, but I know ... the parties had talks with them. "Karadzic: Okay, okay. "Mandic: It will be on radio news now. "Karadzic: Pardon? "Mandic: The announcement will be on the radio too. "Karadzic: Yes, yes. Meet them tonight or tomorrow and explain that the Serbs in eastern Herzegovina could only be concerned for an attack of the Ustasha and that regarding Muslims there will be no problems. "Mandic: I told them that already. "Karadzic: Okay. But issue an announcement too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that during the playing of that intercept the witness was quite actively perusing a binder that's in front of him. I'm guessing that that contains certain exhibits and maybe he was looking for this particular document, but I think we needed to know at the outset what that binder is and the witness should be cautioned about referring to it without alerting the parties to the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, you heard what Mr. Tieger has just said. Could you kindly explain what you are looking at at the moment. What that binder you have with you is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have brought some papers, i.e., some documents from Trebinje. Those are the documents that I have kept from those retched war times. I've just been perusing the binder to see if I've got everything and to get my bearings among all those documents that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I leave it at that or, Mr. Tieger, would you like to take a look at those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, yeah, at some point I want to take a look at it. I think for the moment the best thing to do would simply -- since they, in fact, are not either his statement or the exhibits associated with that which would have been a potentially appropriate reference tool. So I think the witness should be cautioned not to refer to that unless there is some very specific need that he identifies in advance and then we can deal with it in the circumstances that arise at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I take it you have understood Mr. Tieger's point so that I don't need to repeat it. But if you need to take a look at those documents if you could let us know in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Actually, there is a key document that I have brought with me. I would like to show it to you later, so for a moment I was concerned about the whereabouts of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, did you recognise the two interlocutors from Gacko as you were listening to the second intercept?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised one very convincingly. On the one hand we have Mr. President and on the other end of the line there was Vlado Kovacevic, an MP in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on he was an MP in the Assembly of Republika Srpska. I don't know Mandic that well. I don't know what his position was at the time, but I know him by sight and I think that I recognised his voice. He's from Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the topic that we discussed and to what extent are you familiar with the topic in view of the fact that you were a prominent leader not only in east Herzegovina but elsewhere as well but particularly in eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely familiar with the topic because I was present and I was the president of the municipality of Trebinje, and that was actually the principal municipality in eastern Herzegovina settled by a majority Serbian population. Our meetings were numerous. Our discussions were lengthy and extensive, and so on and so forth. I can confirm and I can vouch for that. I can also prove based on the evidence that I have that everything was done for the minority population to leave Herzegovina in peace in order to avoid interethnic conflicts, and there were no such conflicts in Trebinje. When the Muslims received instructions from the top echelons of the SDA - and I have documents on my hands that they would be moving out from Trebinje - I believe that the problem arose and the problem was the fact that in the Trebinje war brigade there were 412 Muslims who are now referred to as Bosniaks. When the Yugoslav People's Army left and they had started the war with Croatian paramilitaries on the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, then the Muslim and Croat forces joined forces. We were concerned. And then the Muslims who were present in the Serbian army were ordered to leave the units because Alija Izetbegovic and the top echelons of the SDA were not happy to see that Muslims were waging a war against Muslims. At that time I decided that everybody who wanted a passport should apply for it and that they would be issued with a passport so that they could travel freely and leave the territory. Those who applied for passes - and I have hundreds of such requests - were issued with passes in the following way: Those who were civilians, they would apply for a pass and they would get a letter of confirmation that they could travel. I apologise. Those who were soldiers had to provide a confirmation that they had returned the equipment and the uniforms that they had been issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucurevic. I would wish to tender these two intercepts into evidence and mark them for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. Do we have the number for them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the numbers that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI is D3171 and MFI D3172 respectively. Your Honours, the 92 ter statement 1D07948 will be Exhibit D3146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for Mr. Vucurevic at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Robinson, para 24 -- no, wait, 25 refers to the intercept, the number of which is 30233 on page 12. Is this intercept referred to in the statement elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think somewhere the statement refers to 65 ter 31953 or 30323, but at the moment I can't find -- locate them. I meant to ask whether they were typos or not. If you found -- find them, please come back to me. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it was at former paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But now they are gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Except that the structure of the statement didn't vary much because a couple of the paragraphs were omitted and then others included. So you would find it in that general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, probably I saw the previous document. Very well. Mr. Vucurevic, as you have noted, your evidence in this case, your evidence in chief, has been admitted in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, we'll have about ten minutes before the first recess, so we will be -- won't be getting too deep into the questions that I have. But before I begin, let me indicate to you that the Court asks us particularly during the cross-examination exchange to be as efficient as possible and asked me to focus on particular issues that I wish to discuss and asks the witness to respond to those questions in the most concise possible way. So by way of example, if I ask you if you have read a particular book, at that point I'm only asking for a yes or no answer, not a description of the contents of that book or a description of the author and so on. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your statement says on the front that you are now a pensioner and were previously -- your previous occupation was official, but as you note in paragraph 1 of your statement you became an official or came to the role of official late in life. What was your occupation before that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I spent most of my career in private business. I got involved in politics only in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you stayed in politics and in an official role until your removal from the position as vice-president of the SDS by the Office of the High Representative in 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And even prior to that time you had been indicted for, among other things, events in the Ravno municipality where 17 or more civilians were killed, many houses destroyed, and civilians of Croatian nationality removed to the Bileca concentration camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To a certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Vucurevic, I want to address what you said in your statement about the Muslims leaving Trebinje in paragraph 19 and paragraph 24 where you assert that their departure was caused by the SDA headquarters and the local Trebinje SDA and then add in paragraph 24 that was in order to make the negotiating position in Geneva more difficult for the Serbs. So before we recess, I wanted to look a little more closely at what people were saying about that departure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection I'd like to call up a certain document. I need the 65 ter for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 24834.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as that's being called up, let me point out that's an article from the independent Montenegrin newspaper, "The Monitor," dated 5 February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Reid could release it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is released, Mr. President. There appears to be further glitches. I mean, it was released before. Mr. Reid just looked at it again, so it may be another e-court problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We also don't have access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, given the time maybe we need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It sounds like something we need to do and check the e-court system again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at three to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, before we recessed we were attempting to look at an article from "The Monitor," that is, the independent Montenegrin newspaper at 24834 and I think we're able to call that up now. Now, this is an article as I mentioned before that's dated the 5th of February. And if you'll take a quick glance at the first two pages of the article, both the cover page and the first page, I think you'll be able to see quickly what the subject is about.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You should now, sir, on the split screen. And if we could turn to the -- there you see the date and if we could turn to the second page of the B/C/S. Now -- and I'll ask you quickly to look at the pass that is shown on that front page. That is a copy depicted in this article of the kinds of passes that you referred to in your statement which you or the Trebinje authorities issued to departing Muslims toward the end of January or beginning of February 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think we can agree that given the date of the article, the location that's described about the people who are the subject of the article, and this pass, that this is an article about the -- or concerning the exodus of the Trebinje Muslims to parts of Montenegro; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You think this is about something entirely different? I'm suggesting to you it's about the same events you describe at, for example, in paragraph 19 of your statement, that is, the departure of the Muslim community from Trebinje in late January and early December 1993. That's the subject matter of this article; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The subject is quite a different thing from what actually happened on the ground. That was the era of the JNA's dominance. Before that I wasn't able to respond to what was happening in Ravno and everything was in the hands in the GNA, and the civilian authorities were not consulted about anything. The army had come from Montenegro just like this paper comes from Montenegro as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vucurevic, maybe you'll understand my question a bit better if I describe for you what is being discussed in the article, and in it we find excerpts from precisely what people who had left Trebinje were explaining to "The Monitor." So, for example, and you should be -- if we scrolled down on the first page for your benefit -- and the pages shown for your benefit, or actually turn to the second page, please, to the next page after that. We see various accounts by people. For example, Mr. Mujo Malohodzic describes the disarming of Muslims, the burning of the mosque, threats by telephone, forcible entry of houses. Another departing Muslim talks about being abused physically by the police. One person -- same person describes speaking with you and who advised him that you don't need to go but I don't guarantee for anybody's life. Other people talk about the police coming and waiting to take possession of their homes and so on. And one person, Mr. Adjalic [phoen], addresses the issue that is raised in your statement at paragraph 19, that is, the allegation that people were leaving their homes because the SDA told them to? And he said as you can see toward the bottom of the first column on the page that is shown: "All men not older than 60 years old were on the front for 18 months at the most. We had to shoot at Muslims and Croats." That's something you -- and I stop the quote for a second. That's something you alluded to earlier in terms of the participation of Muslims in the Herzegovina Corps. Now I continue the quote: "Now we don't have any place in Bosnia or Croatia. Maybe the best would be if you kill us here. We wouldn't leave our homes and riches just to come here and to sleep on floors just because of Izetbegovic's politics as Bozidar Vucurevic has accused us of. The only property we have now is travel bags or garbage bags." Now, these contemporaneous accounts by people who had left Trebinje and shown up in Montenegro describe the pressures and force to which they were subjected and also deal with the allegation that people would leave their homes, their riches, their entrenched lives because of a political interest. That's the reality of the situation, isn't it, Mr. Vucurevic, that the Muslims of Trebinje, many of whom as you said served in the Herzegovina Corps, were not Islamic fanatics who would abandon their lives simply because of the interest of some politician, but instead were forced out by the pressures to which they were subjected?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No. Everybody can make accusations but they need to provide proof. By taking over Trebinje and subjecting it to the command of the 1st Military District, here we have an order issued by the National Defence Secretariat from Belgrade, instructing us to become subordinated to the 1st Military District. General-Lieutenant Aleksandar Mitkovski [phoen] was the one who installed a mobilisation organ in Trebinje and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat part of the answer that we couldn't catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: How can I say it otherwise? I can say either yes or no and I say no, this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, you were speaking too fast for the interpreters to catch up, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's all right. The mobilisation organ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, if you could start from General Lieutenant Aleksandar Mitkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I understand the problem with speed, but it also seems -- the witness also seems to be addressing an entirely unrelated subject now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you take up again, then. Please put your question again, then, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I am focusing on what happened at the end of January and beginning of February 1993 when virtually the entire or at least the bulk of the Trebinje Muslim population was - as they say - forced out but certainly departed for Montenegro. I am not asking you about the mobilisation order at a time when the JNA was still in Bosnia. So please focus on the question. I read to you excerpts from "The Monitor" article. People who arrived in Montenegro with garbage bags or travel bags and had left their homes completely behind and what they said about why that had happened. And I put it to you that that was a more accurate account of what had happened than what is contained in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: When the Municipal Board of the Party of Democratic Action received an instruction from the top leadership of their party and the instruction related to the people moving out of Trebinje, I received about 500 Muslims in a municipal hall and there we discussed and agreed the issue of safety and security. I told them that nobody was forcing them out, but that also on the other hand nobody could guarantee them safety. Why? Because 15.400 refugees arrived in Trebinje from other parts and that the Serbs became a minority. There was an uncontrolled arming of the people. My cousin was killed by Serbs. So I couldn't guarantee his life, let alone the lives of the entire population. They were told either to remain with us or to comply with the instruction issued by Alija Izetbegovic, or rather, the Secretary-General Hasan Cengic. They opted for the latter option. They sought passes to be issued to them and they asked the army to demobilise their men. Whoever asked to leave was given permission with escort and complete safety. Those who remained behind did not come into harm's way in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there was an investigation undertaken at the time of the events that were taking place, and I want to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But in order to do so, Mr. President, we'll have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as -- this is -- this seems to implicate the book report versus whether or not you read the book, guidance I provided at the outset. So I'd like to know when you claim you first found out about this alleged order from the SDA Sarajevo and SDA Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon when I was at home, I was called by a Muslim who asked to see me somewhere but not in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, before -- I'm sorry, before you get to the entire description, I want to -- I'm looking for a chronology so that's what I'm trying to focus on. So we could -- have seen from the previous discussion that you claim to be aware of an SDA effort to urge Muslims to lead -- to leave by at least early February or late January when you spoke to the persons in the document we looked at in private session. I'd like to know when you claim you first came into possession of the document from the SDA Sarajevo and the SDA Trebinje? When was that? Early January? Late January? Early February? Late February? 1993? 1994? When did you get ahold of the document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Somewhat previously I believe, although I do not recall the exact date, but it's in the document and it was preserved. I received a call from a Muslim -- actually, there were two. One of them told me that he was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDA. He also confessed to me that they had received instructions from Hasan Cengic, the general secretary, and that later the local Municipal Board drafted some sort of order to leave Trebinje. He had a few sheets of paper folded in his jacket and he asked me to assist him to get out safely with his family as well as to take his car with him. In return, he wanted to give me the papers they had received and they are part of the documentation here, where it is irrefutably proven that it was done under instruction of the SDA with its seat in Sarajevo and it was implemented through the Municipal Board in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's go into private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up 65 ter 24818.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And tender the previous document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, probably after showing the document in private session the questions could be put in open session. Think about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President, and I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6224 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, it would help us to assess the relevance of these questions, and while that we don't object to the documents, to know whether the Prosecution has any dispute about the authenticity of Exhibit D471, which is the instruction from the SDA 20th of January, 1993, for the Muslims to leave Trebinje, or whether it's their position that that is authentic but the Muslims ignored that order. I wonder if Mr. Tieger could tell us what the Prosecution's position is on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to affirm its authenticity, and frankly some of the circumstances that have been related during the course of this morning would suggest otherwise, but insofar as Trebinje is not an indictment municipality this is not a matter we've been in a position to address in the detail we're going into it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I think that's very helpful to us to note because we have, as you know, filed a motion to subpoena Hasan Cengic, the author of this document. So I think that the Prosecution's position helps us make that issue more clear and I appreciate Mr. Tieger addressing it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I've also addressed in private -- as long as we're talking about it, if we're in private [sic] session, some of the factors that make that not the most relevant matter, but anyway we can deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I had asked you a moment ago about your characterisation of the Muslims of Trebinje not as a group of professionals, family people, normal, good people, but instead as religious fanatics leaving in lock-step with the orders of their political leadership and happily doing so, and you essentially denied that that had been the case. I wanted to call up 65 ter 24820A at time code 7.44 through 9.17. And this is a transcript in English of what you said in a lengthy interview that was conducted about 20 months after the war began when you were on a -- I think a epic poetry or book tour in Belgrade. And there you said the following -- speaking about the departure of the Muslims and the -- your allegation that people had left because they were invited to do so by Izetbegovic. First of all, you spoke about the fact that Muslims had a great deal of wealth. How, you say? Because these were sons of beys, rich beys from the Ottoman era who had large properties, who had properties by the river of the -- of Trebisnjica, large houses, et cetera, et cetera. And then you say it is -- this -- this is on e-court page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 3, e-court page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "It is hard to believe," you say or you said then, "but when they received the message to leave, they left singing in the buses, they had left everything they had behind them carrying with them only bundles or backpacks and they were singing in buses. That could not happen to my people. That is an example of religious fanaticism." And you continue to say a message from Allah was mentioned there, that Allah had sent word, and you contrast that again with Serbs, that is a kind of fanaticism, et cetera. So, Mr. Vucurevic, contrary to your assertion a moment ago, you did try to depict the departure of Muslims from Trebinje as being the joyous implementation of an order executed by religious fanatics; right? That's how you subsequently described the event?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you want to hear your own words, Mr. Vucurevic? Do you deny that you said this? Because you're on tape.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, esteemed sirs, all of those who wanted to prevent bloodshed in Trebinje and who wanted to secure that Muslims left individually at first and then in small groups and then in the large groups, they were provided buses and escort and transportation. That was very joyous, as contrasted against the plight of Serbs in Sarajevo and elsewhere. It was all song and dance compared to other situations when people lost their family, et cetera. But we also had to appease our own people. Fire was opened on my own house and there is a record of on-site investigation. It was probably done by my own Serbs because they thought I was protecting Muslims. One was not supposed to speak positively and you had to count on your own people as well. It was a skill and one needed to go back and forth all in order to avoid bloodshed. That is what I actually intended to say and I'm proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that excerpt, Mr. President. There will be some more as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering only this part of the transcript or are you also tendering the clip -- is it video or the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I think both would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But whether you can identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, this transcript and I'm happy to tender the -- I think it's useful to tender the excerpt as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move on to another subject in the interests of time, sir. Now, you've spoken about the police of Trebinje particularly in 1993 a number of times, and of course it is the police who were supposed to be protecting the Muslims of Trebinje; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn to 1D25798. That probably has an exhibit number by now and I don't have the corresponding reference, but it was the previous 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D3162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to turn to page 10 of the English and that would be page -- it should be the same in the B/C/S. And this is another conversation you had with Mr. Karadzic. The two of you were talking and he says to you: "Bozo I am," this is at the bottom of page 10 in the English and toward the middle of the page 10 in the B/C/S. "Bozo, I am, I am. I do not know how this Borkovic works for you. I don't think he is not working well?" And you say: "No, no, he is serious."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Can you tell him -- I mean, things have moved on too far. We will have complete control over things. Will he be loyal or will he not be?" And then you go on to describe how he lost face the other day at the council, that is, which -- the National Defence Council which has taken on the role of the Crisis Staff. And then the conversation regarding Mr. Borkovic continues and, as we see at page 12 of the English and B/C/S, Mr. Karadzic says: "Does he know what time it is? Does he know this is a historical moment?" And you say: "Well, I believe he will have to -- he will have to get serious." And Mr. Karadzic says: "Let that happen soon, let that be very soon because I have obtained approval for a security centre to open there. We will receive support from some forces ..." Now, Mr. Borkovic was chief of police at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: For a very brief period of time. Borkovic was with the police for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this conversation where Mr. Karadzic says "things have moved on too far. We will have complete control over things" took place on the 9th of January, 1992, just a few days before the extended sitting of the Main and Executive Boards on 14 February 1992, which you attended and which is also referenced in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's -- if you recall that excerpt, that's the meeting at which you spoke for some time about events in the late 1300s and early 1400s in Dubrovnik where a number of dukets were exchanged or not exchanged and that gave rise to your argument that Dubrovnik should be disputed internationally. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many events. It's hard to remember all of them, so I cannot confirm that I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's contained in the -- did you not read that recently, because that's contained as part of the your statement and was one of the associated exhibits that were supposedly provided as part of the statement that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that that was in the press? In the press?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vucurevic, I'm saying that you provided a statement to this Court. It references that meeting and provides as an associated exhibit to that statement the remarks I just mentioned to you from the session of 14 February. Could you -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you let us know the para number of witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was previously -- I think it's still currently in 32. It was previously in paragraph 31, I believe, but I think it's -- yeah, it is 32, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it you haven't seen that lately, Mr. Vucurevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you more broadly about that session --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. The interpreter could not hear him nor could she interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, they didn't hear you. I asked you if you'd -- I said you hadn't seen that lately, correct, and your answer was ... ?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, at -- you did indicate in your statement, Mr. Vucurevic, that you attended that session and we have evidence of what happened at that session, including the fact - and this is found at P00012 - that it was at that session that Dr. Karadzic activated the second level of Variant A and B, referring to it at least four separate times. Do you recall that, Mr. Vucurevic, because you didn't mention that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just give you a couple of references that Dr. Karadzic made at that time. At the bottom of page 5 of P0012, that is, if you remember, who keeps that in mind, or maybe not on his person, a stage number two, there is -- you remember what I'm talking about, from the audience we know, yes. That is, therefore, the stage number two, the second stage in smaller or bigger variations, but you have to implement that slowly now to have absolute control who is travelling along your roads, et cetera. And just one more reference at page 24, and as regards the essence of which Mr. Radic spoke now: "Please, that is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and in every single millimetre of our territory." Does that recall your recollection of Mr. Karadzic's references to Variant A and B and the introduction of the second level within a very short time after you had talked with him about the fact that this was a historical moment and that we will have complete control over things?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about Variants, I'm aware of only two Variants which existed from the beginning of the conflict until the end of the war. Mr. Karadzic was aware of them and they were implemented by the Main Board down. If we cannot live together, we should split in peace. And if everything else fails, we have to defend ourselves. I don't know of any other variant but these two that prevailed all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Tieger. Having difficulty following the witness statement again. You referred to paragraph 32 where the witness said about his statement in a session. Could we upload his statement para 32? What I have with me is what I have -- I'm seeing at the e-court, but I'm not sure if that's the one you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, if it helps, I definitely have that in the previous version by the witness that is -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic confirmed it was para 32, yes, because you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, and it is. It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this it, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think the exhibit is an excerpt reflecting the witness's comments at that session. That's what it purports to be and that's what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- which is why I described some of the details the witness went into at that time involving the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But 1D25791 is an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I read 1D25802, Mr. President. Okay, it is -- I've got, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry about this. I've got three different versions. The first draft, then something that was submitted as the final version, and then the -- then now this third version which does have the same -- the precise words of what I had been previously saying was at paragraph 32 in paragraph 36: "I have been shown document 1D25802." And I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I have difficulty in locating that document. Where is it referred to in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- as far as I'm aware, it's referred to at page -- I mean, looking at it right here, I've got -- here's the version I printed out most recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It refers to paragraph 32, 1D25802. Here's what -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this is the -- this -- what we are seeing on the monitor is to be the most recent version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here is what I understand is the most recent version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- which has the same paragraph at paragraph 36, and then if we want turn to paragraph 36 here, if it's not there, then I don't know what happened in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was a bit confused all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President. I should not have [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the old version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, this is now the latest version. It conforms to the previous latest version and the original proposed final was -- had this at paragraph 32 which is where the confusion arise -- arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm actually a little confused also, because we only know of two versions, the original witness statement that was disclosed early on, part of our 65 ter obligations, and then the statement which was e-mailed to everyone on Friday which is the same one that we're all using today. So I'm not understanding why there's more than two versions that Mr. Tieger has. But anyway, you have the latest version that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, and the confusion may be that one is a track changes version. That may be the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. You did confirm that Mr. Borkovic was for some period of time the chief of police in Trebinje and we took a look at what -- at the discussion that you and Mr. Karadzic had about him in February in 1992. I'd like to look at -- by the way, you said that Mr. Borkovic was there only for a short time. Why did he leave?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He arrived on the eve of the war. He had fled from Zenica. He was praised as a good worker. He was chief for a few months. When things took off the ground, when things escalated, he fled to Belgrade. He was there for a very short period of time. I don't know exactly for how long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm confused. I don't know whether Mr. Tieger gives up on the thesis that in paragraph 36 there is a reference to the meeting which took place on the 14th of February, 1992. A lot was recorded and I fail to see any link.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to explain if the Court has any -- confusion by the Court, but I don't think there is. This witness was present at the meeting on February 14th, and I confronted him with what else was said at that same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If I can move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness statement itself does not make much reference to this meeting. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic -- oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Tieger. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Except that both documents reflect the witness's presence at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, let's see if I can refresh your memory about why Mr. Borkovic left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 24836.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a statement given to the ICTY by Mr. Borkovic. He also identifies himself as the -- at one time the chief of police in Trebinje, and he describes at the top of page 4 how his departure from that position took place. He notes that in early January he was ordered by the authorities to ethnically cleanse the police from Muslims. They wanted only Serbs as police officers and he refused to do so. And when he says "authorities," he means Krsto Savic, the chief of police in Nevesinje, but who had also been appointed as the chief of police of the SAO Herzegovina in September/October 1991. And your statement identifies you as the president of the SAO Trebinje Hercegovina, Mr. Vucurevic. Mr. Borkovic indicates that he -- thereafter he attended a meeting with other chiefs of police that took place in your office. The other chiefs were talking about how they cleansed their forces. These were chiefs from Ljubinje, Gacko, Ilica, and Nevesinje, and at that meeting he was dismissed as the chief of police in Trebinje, and it was decided that Krsto Savic should temporarily take over his post. On the next day, Krsto Savic entered his office with several armed men and he was thrown out. All the Muslim police officers were dismissed from their jobs by Krsto Savic on the same day, and he goes on to describe Mr. Savic as a nationalist, chauvinist, and very rough in his attitude against Muslims and Croats. Mr. Vucurevic, that's a more fulsome and more accurate account of how Mr. Borkovic left his position as chief of police in Trebinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No. Gentlemen, when -- people needed to be promoted once there had already been a split in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the Serbian MUP had to be promulgated, Mr. Karadzic expressly ordered the then-minister of the interior - the name escapes me but now I remember Mr. Stanisic - that everybody who received a new uniform could stay with the police and could keep --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic -- Mr. Vucurevic, you're talking --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: -- his position that he had previously had --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're talking about a later time. I'm asking you about the specific circumstances. If you deny that Mr. -- the allegations made here, and particularly that Mr. Borkovic was forced out because he refused to ethnically cleanse the police or that Mr. Savic was someone rough in his attitude against Muslims and Croats, that's your position.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: If I have the right not to agree, but I absolutely do not agree. Mr. Borkovic had fled from Zenica. His only son and his wife remained in Zenica. They subsequently fled to Belgrade. He abandoned his position. He did not have a successor. Nobody had chased him away. Nobody had given him any inappropriate tasks. He simply joined his wife and son without ever reporting to anybody, so there could not be any talk about an order given to Borkovic to implement something that was inhumane. He never reported to anybody before he left and people went on looking for him for several days after he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, the fact is that although you've been depicting yourself as someone with a great deal of benevolence toward the Muslims, the reality is that you were someone who was determined to see separation, that you were concerned about the ethnic structure in Republika Srpska being to the disadvantage of the Serbs, and in general you thought that there was a -- and were concerned about the birth-rate of Muslims as a result and referred to this miserable Islam and described a civilisational war. All of those things are actually true about your attitude rather than how you've been depicting yourself as the benevolent leader of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: If I were allowed to do so I would ask you, if Trebinje was the only city in Bosnia-Herzegovina when -- where there were no inter-ethnic conflicts, where not even the smallest house was burned, where no property was destroyed, where the Muslims returned from Denmark predominantly to spend holidays there and who thanked me, and they did it in the presence of the International Red Cross - I have a document to that effect where they thanked me - and if I achieved that in Trebinje as it was, and now you are trying to blame me, either you or somebody else, for behaving in a humane and civilisational way, then all of this is nothing short of a sheer wonder to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vucurevic, we've already addressed the pillar you seem to be relying upon, that everything in Trebinje went so swimmingly, but I'm actually focusing on the expression of your attitudes toward such issues as ethnic separation, ethnic structure, birth-rates, and the Muslim or Islamic civilisation generally. So let's look at a few of those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all 65 ter 24813. This should be an article from ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"" in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It begins with as you can see toward the bottom your excellent relations with -- or your former excellent relations with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and whether or not you're still in touch with him. You recall providing that information to ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"" back in 1994, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I am 80 years of age and the letters are too small for me to read, but I can confirm that I have read dozens of my interviews that I never gave to anybody. At that time the war was waged in all sorts of ways. There was a war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, let's be --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: -- waged with rifles and there was a media war. So I've read a number of my interviews --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"" conducting a media war against you? That's a Serbian organ; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can see your picture on the screen in front of you. This is an October 1994 edition of ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a little bit the witness can see the heading and -- further down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"" was a Bosnian Serb organ; right? And they weren't conducting a media war against you, sir, were they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it all depended. From time to time they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
