utterances.text: All right. Well, I -- we looked at the -- it's a big picture of you. Are you accustomed to having your picture on the cover or the pages of ""Srpsko Oslobodjenje"" on a daily basis or do you remember that you gave such an interview to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you that I cannot read these small letters so I cannot see what is contained in the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why can't we remove the English page from the screen because it is actually not a translation of the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has obviously been doctored in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the time I'm wondering if we could print this out for the witness and during the lunch break he could have a chance to read it over and then maybe he could answer more authoritatively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you need, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I have left is the items I indicated I'd have. I want to cover quickly three intercepts that were taken out of the earlier draft so that the Court -- which were basically authenticated by this witness were taken out. So I want to get those introduced. And then I have one more matter related to Dubrovnik. So I would say about -- assuming we get through this quickly, I would say about 25 minutes. I realise that I'm at the time allotted, but it's -- I think sometimes difficult to tell when the allocations are made what the witness will be like or what kinds of evidence -- what kind of information will be relevant to his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from the issue, would it cause much problem if the Chamber is to take a lunch break for an hour and adjourn at 3.00 today, only for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then when we adjourn, I would like you to try to conclude in 15 minutes, give it a try. The Chamber will break for an hour and resume at 1.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Two quick things. It turns out that I was not responsible for the confusion of the paragraphs, as Mr. Robinson graciously advised me. And as a result we had a conversation about moving through the remaining portion of the examination much more efficiently and I'm grateful to the Defence for that discussion and the approach that we'll take -- that we'll follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I see you have the article in front of you now, that is the "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" article. As you have been able to see, that article discusses -- in the course of that interview with "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" you discuss a number of things, including contacts with Milosevic, the rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan, access to the sea, and so on. So before I go on, I take it that having the opportunity to review that refreshed your recollection about having given such an interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this conversation never happened. Please. The war started and then it was left up to one municipality, Trebinje, to finish it off. We were very angry with the state of Yugoslavia for initiating all this. Since I am a poet and a writer, it contains some pejorative comments, and then you have a title "We are not Going to Attack Serbia With Stones," especially that someone took great care to put this frightening picture of me which obviously makes it something that has been apparently doctored.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, difficult to tell precisely what you're referring to, sir, but let me take you to a particular -- let me ask you, and before I do that, let me ask you if you were aware of the fact that "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" was an -- a publication enterprise that was created by a decision of the Republika Srpska government in April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it was praised by people such as Momcilo Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: But this cannot be a guarantee that they would do something well-intentionally at every point and in every place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just go to the portion of the article toward -- on the last page of that article, where you are quoted as saying the following, after discussing negotiations with Croatia and, more specifically, with Mate Boban and you say: "They will part ways very soon and this is a good thing too," meaning the Croats and the Muslims. That was your position at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I met with Mate Boban, a Croatian leader, because we were two neighbouring peoples in eastern Herzegovina. Now, what was the purpose of that meeting? It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, no, Mr. Vucurevic, let's focus on one thing at a time. It was your position at the time that this "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" article that the Muslims and the Croats would part ways very soon and you considered that a good thing, right? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you thought it would be a good thing if the Muslims and the stayed together, you thought that would be a good thing?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Everything was in the function of stopping war escalation between the Serbs and Croats that were quite fierce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here is what you're quoted as saying in the article with reference to parting -- those parting of the ways. "That should suit us so that we can also sort out the Muslims once and for all. You see, to have anything to do with the Muslims is like dealing with the devil himself. Let me tell you, this war with them, it is no longer only a religious, ethnic, and civil war or whatever they call it. This is a civilisational war. This miserable Islam, this civilisation of theirs is about to explode. The way they breed, you cannot even count them. Their birth-rate, God help us all, and they have no land or country of their own. That is why the Croats are afraid of being with them." Now, Mr. Vucurevic, that was the expression of your views in 1994; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation is completely worthless. First of all, the English translation read by Mr. Tieger. Therefore, I would kindly ask that this paragraph be put to the witness regardless of whether he said it in a pub or in an interview. The fact remains that it was mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm happy to get it retranslated, but I understood the witness was -- okay, fair enough if the witness was hearing other words, but let's make sure we're talking about the same portion of the article. Please call up -- I think we have that last page there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you can see the portion we're talking about, sir, which is the second column and the last -- the bottom paragraph that is not in italics. Now, that's the portion of the interview to which I was drawing your attention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not translated to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the witness is reading it now. He can tell us whether this portion first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we identify the portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because it's in Cyrillic I'm not going to be able to phonetically read it, but the cursor -- if you move the cursor slightly to the right, it's that portion and up. It's that portion of the article, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, could you read the portion which you see in front of you? If you could read aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can openly tell you that I was able to reach an agreement with Mato Boban about many things despite the war. Listen, they do not like the Muslims. What are you talking about? It is the pressure that the Americans and the Germans are exerting on them and causing them enormous troubles, but they will part their -- they will go their separate ways very soon. Well, let them do it. This will be beneficial to us as well so that we separate from Muslims for once and for all because -- I told you, all of this was an insinuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you're wondering, Mr. President, the witness stopped before completing the rest of the paragraph which contains the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could -- could you read out the paragraph, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can read it. Because, if you are in a league with the Muslims it is just like being in a league with the devil, but I want to tell you this war with them is no longer only a religious and a national or a civil war as somebody would like to call it. This is the war of civilisations. This retched Islam and this civilisation is on the brink of being exploded and they are breeding. You cannot count them. They have an enormous birth-rate and not all the countries have enough space and that is why the Croats are afraid of being in league with them. I read this paragraph but I have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I would tender that and I'd move on to some taped comments by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't object to this being admitted, although the issue of weight is important since the witness hasn't confirmed that it was his -- that he said those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still believe that we have a translation issue of the attributes used with regard of Islam. The word was not "miserable" but rather "unfortunate" or something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was -- I think "miserable" was in the original translation, "retched" was in the translation we heard a moment ago. The difference is not particularly significant in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I wanted to ask you about a certain number of things you said during that taped interview we discussed earlier. The first one, and that is 65 ter -- or it's now P6225, and so I'll be asking to append these additional portions to that exhibit. I'll run through them as quickly as I can, Mr. Vucurevic, for your benefit and for the benefit of the Court. First at excerpt 00:15:35 through 17:42 you stated the following: "I mean, it is true when they say that Serbs are to blame for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- actually, they are because they started it between themselves, both Croats and Muslims were Serbs in the past, you know. They are Catholicised Serbs, Islamised Serbs and such. So why did this happen? I think there is nothing worse than estranging oneself from ones genus. You see, the wolf and the dog are of the same species yet they bite at each other terribly." Then you also noted at 39:47 through 42:33 the following: "Mr. Izetbegovic, that tragic figure in the Muslim nation, has been refusing to give up the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina for a long time, something we shall never agree to for as long as we live because in it we see no happiness, no perspective for our people. We have to put our boots on. We want to build a Serbian state and we will not take those boots off until we have made it." And then: "We have no right to the price. We have no right to count the dead either. With all due respect to our fallen soldiers and those who are yet to fall, we shall not take the boots off. We shall make the Serbian state at any cost. There is no doubt about that." And then finally with respect to the Serbian state you say at 00:20 through 00:1:05: "Yes, this time they will definitely not stop us. We will persevere at all costs and we will make the Serbian state. We will make Republika Srpska a state, and we will, of course, seek annexation to other states. Actually, I think it would be better to call it united Serbian lands and not states." Mr. Vucurevic, those are reflections of comments you made during the -- not reflections, those are the comments you made during the course of your taped interview that we referred to earlier at 6225, that is, the interview that took place in the latter -- the interview taken place in the 20 months after the war began and was part of your book promotion in Belgrade? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: For five centuries we were enslaved by the Turks and lots of Serbs converted to Islam. So one can indeed say this was a war between the Catholicised Serbs, the Islamised Serbs, and those who remained Orthodox. That was one nation and it was such a big misfortune that they fought war against each other and that was our misfortune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those excerpts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add those parts to the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, you referred to negotiations with Mate Boban, a discussion about those negotiations are found at 65 ter 24818 -- 815, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban as the leader of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president of the HDZ invited me to come to Grude in the war zone were populated by the Croats. I took a risk and I went to see him so that the two of us can do something and stop the war and the bloodshed. And we were almost on the brink of reaching an agreement, but regrettably we failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we see on the front page of this article a photograph of the two of you that reflects those discussions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: This is not Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies. This was the journalist you were talking to at the time. If you could look quickly at the bolded portion, for example, just to confirm that this was a discussion about those -- about that meeting with Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what secret negotiations are being discussed here. If you are making a statement to the press, then it's not secret at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, during the course of those discussions with Mate Boban, the issue of borders, not surprisingly, came up. And Boban asked you your view of where the border should go, and you proposed what you considered the most natural one, that is, the Neretva river; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said to Boban, so it would be Croats to the west and Serbs to the east of the Neretva, and then Boban asked -- or then, as did the reporter, asked you: Well, is there a place for the Muslims there? And your response to Boban was that the place for the Muslims, that is, this semi-nation, is in between, that is, in the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Ah, no, definitely not. No way. On the other side the majority were Croats and the Serbs were on the opposite side, and I told him if we cannot do it together let us stop the war. Let us be good neighbours and co-operate. Now, as for this comment about the Muslims, this is a fabrication. Somebody made that up. Anyway, there were only a few of them living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So -- and the -- so you're saying the journalist made up the fact that you said in the Neretva both Boban and I laughed at my response, et cetera, and that's found in the last column, sir. Can we blow that up and go to the last column, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Tieger kindly not -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The top part of that column, please. The second response, if we could blow that up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that, but I do not accept that. I wouldn't say that in a dream. What journalists are making up, it's their problem, I mean this comment about the Muslims being in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. Again, with respect to the issue of what he said, it would be a matter of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were three intercepts that were part of the original package of the amalgamated statement and that were associated exhibits and that were obviously during the course of that process authenticated by the witness since they involve him. And I would, with the agreement of the Defence as mentioned before, I would tender those, that's 65 ter 30183, 1D25793, and 1D25794.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have they been commented on in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, they all arose out of paragraph 24, Mr. President, where he gave an explanation of general events in Trebinje and issues that arose and then those intercepts were to -- were examples of the information that he provided. That's how they were originally packaged in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If this witness has authenticated the intercept, it may be a subject of bar table motion. If you are not leading those intercepts with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court gives me some time to go ahead and do that, I'm happy to do so. I just thought this was a more efficient way in light of the fact that there had been general comments about him and the circumstances in which they originally arose. It seems -- I don't mean to make this a particular practice, but in this case it seemed a quite efficient and appropriate way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how do we analyse whether it is relevant in what context to the case? I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, these did -- let me -- I'm sorry, Mr. President, if it helps, these are all conversations between the witness and Mr. Karadzic in -- and the earlier comments were about personnel matters, interaction between the witness and the accused in connection with some of those matters. So I think we know the context now in which they arise from the statement. I think paragraph 24 continued to remain in the statement, but these particular intercepts were omitted. I mean, if I had more time I would actually pursue the issue of why they had been omitted and some of the specifics, but I don't think that that undercuts their relevance in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Speaking from our side, we would also like to have these admitted. They were dropped from the statement because I instructed our person who was working with this witness to reduce the amount of associated exhibits to make it more manageable for the Chamber and he did that by eliminating some of these intercepts, but we think they're relevant. We think they're admissible because the witness is one of the participants so that they wouldn't need to be marked for identification or further authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As D, please. It should be admitted as D exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it -- as far as I'm concerned it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them as P exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P6227 [sic] through to Exhibits P6230 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that's a better solution. Then we shall refer to Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's from Exhibit P6228.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6228 through P6230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And one last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, you have further topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just -- sorry, Mr. President, just very quickly, and it just involves -- this will be very short I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, if you can confirm that in fact you are -- among the things you're known for in the region was being -- was saying with respect to the -- to Dubrovnik and the controversy surrounding the shelling of Dubrovnik that we will build a more beautiful and older Dubrovnik. That's the topic you were asked about by the interviewer during the course of your -- the interview we've spoken of before?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as the shelling of Dubrovnik is concerned, the civilian authorities have nothing to do with it. As for the statement itself mentioned here, gentlemen, the Croats demolished the old bridge on the Neretva river, a renowned historical monument. When they asked them why they did it, they said that they would build a new bridge on the Neretva river. When I was surprised to have heard them saying that, if they claim that they would be able to build an older bridge, I repeated the same with regard to Dubrovnik. But I think that was not a serious matter. That was said jokingly and therefore I don't take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the bridge was mentioned first it should say "a new and older bridge" because that was the paradox involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what you also said about Dubrovnik is captured at 22:33 through 26:30, and in particular the latter portion of that of 6225 when you said as follows in connection with the shelling of Dubrovnik. First, as you described earlier in the day, you referred generically to the principle of tit for tat and you talked about Trebinje being shelled and so Dubrovnik being shelled as a result. And then at the end of that you said, when asked where exactly did you shoot, you said: "Please, we shot whatever could be shot at and with as much frequency in Dubrovnik. I mean, yes. And we regret it. We regret every time a missile hits off the target or is fired in vain, but this" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it shown in the Serbian as well so that the witness could see it himself, otherwise we just have a jumble of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is it necessary or relevant to lead with this about Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- I would say the relevance appears -- I was going to move very quickly after introducing this to the accused's awareness of that and his invocation of that as reflected in another article of "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" in January of 1995, where he spoke about the ability of the Bosnian Serbs to target Dubrovnik and used it as leverage against the Croats in negotiations. So for that reason I thought it was relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it have anything to do with the current indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not a geographic focus of the indictment, but I would say the practice reflected in the two examples I was focusing on and attempting to introduce is certainly a matter that we see over and over again during the course of this evidence. But if the Court thinks it's geographic -- that the fact that it's not specifically geographically mentioned in the indictment is an issue, I will say no, of course Dubrovnik is not part of this current indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could kindly move on or conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But time-wise it's also not defined, then perhaps we should refer to 1941 rather than 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Inappropriate, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. If I could conclude with just getting an affirmation by the witness about that portion of the taped transcript that will be adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I could just continue, you said: "This time when they repeated the shelling after five and a half months we returned twice as hard. Next time it happens, we'll fire four times more missiles on Dubrovnik than they fire on Trebinje." Okay. If you can --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we keep going and insisting on this, despite your decision not to do so, can we have this page displayed so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: E-court page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's conclude without seeing that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thank you, Witness, for answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. I have to shed light on a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell the Chamber what is this newspaper, "Nacional"? Where was it published and what was its position vis-a-vis the Serbs, especially in 1997 which is the date of the article? Did you hear me, Mr. Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know who the question was intended for. What did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what is this "Nacional," where is it published, and what was its position concerning the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I've read quite a lot of press, but I've never read "Nacional." I don't know whose publication it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This refers to both the "Nacional" and "Oslobodjenje" articles. Did you indeed give the interviews and were they sent back to you to be authorised and checked?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when the first preliminary agreement was reached to have three Bosnia and Herzegovinas in one?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'll be right on the date, but I know the sequence of events. But I'm afraid I can't be precise in terms of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But today some words were quoted to you from the plenary session of the SDS of the 14th of February, 1992. Do you recall that -- or perhaps we should have the document displayed. Do you remember me saying at the time something about what was achieved and that you should keep it so that there would be no exodus from our parts?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I remember it. I was present, Mr. President. I know that it was all aimed in the direction of achieving an agreement by peaceful means if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've already answered this. The permits to leave, you said that they contained such words that they designated one's right to return. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as per oral agreement with 5- or 600 Muslims in the hall of our Assembly, it was agreed that they would send a delegation to my office where we discussed things as civilised men so that they would choose what to do. We had reached an agreement with the corps command that there would be no soldiers forced to serve. If there were Muslims mobilised in the Serb army, either before or after that date, if such a person did not wish to remain in the ranks, they would be left having first returned their weapons and equipment. Then they would need to submit an application on a form to issue them with a passport, and when we ran out of forms they were issued passes. On the passes it was stated that they could leave Republika Srpska and return freely. I have over 700 samples of such passes which I had issued. They all state the phrase "they are free to return," and those who wished to leave temporarily, that's what we put down. If somebody wanted to take their car with them, we would note the registration plate on the form and could leave; however, that is something that the Serb people in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not do, at least they were not treated the way we treated the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During examination-in-chief there were some allegations of sorts about your position concerning Muslims. Were there significant examples of Serb and Muslim friendship in Trebinje? Did we have some kind of arrangements with certain Muslim parties?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: When the armed conflict or near armed conflict broke out, we tried to calm down the situation in Herzegovina and not Herzegovina alone so that the war would not escalate. At the time the president of the Muslim Bosniak organisation, Mr. Adil -- perhaps you can assist me - Zulfikarpasic or something, we agreed on something. We organised a march of friendship which was a column of vehicles, toured the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and returned to the soccer pitch in Trebinje. 15.000 people gathered there. Mr. Zulfikarpasic spoke there as well as Mr. Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, and myself. We all invited the people to be unified so that we could be saved from being pushed into the war. It seemed we had achieved something, but Mr. Izetbegovic took care to bury it and the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked not to speak directly into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there some footage from the rally at the Leotar soccer pitch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second, Mr. Vucurevic, yes, Mr. Vucurevic, please put a pause before you start answering the question, and then you are speaking too closely to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat from the start. In order to calm the situation down so that there would be no interethnic conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've answered that part. How about the part whether there was any footage of the rally with the 15.000 people? And you can sit back and speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I will. I'm not sure if there's any footage. I can try to check with the voice of Trebinje or Radio Trebinje; however, every speech of every person who spoke there, including Zulfikarpasic, Karadzic, Koljevic, and myself, is there. We all invited all the three peoples to be tolerant and peaceful so that we wouldn't have another bloody war for the third time in the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you were asked about a document that was not admitted but it's in the transcript. There is quite some mention of your position concerning Dubrovnik. Did you support the shelling of Dubrovnik or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President -- yes, I need to wait. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, normally I would invite -- enjoy that question because it opens the door to precisely the portion of the interview that I wasn't able to get in, so out of fairness I'm alerting the Chamber and the Defence to precisely that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show P5749 where it is clearly stated he was against any shelling, and it is an intercept which is on the Prosecution list. They could have offered it in their cross-examination, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 36, line 10, when you discussed the destruction of mosques and churches, you said that the army destroyed it. Did you have in mind a specific unit and whether it was ordered -- well, I know what you had in mind but do tell us what you had in mind when you said the army destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: A unit arrived in Trebinje gradually, not as a single group, but they took up their headquarters in the Leotar hotel, causing much trouble for us. I sent to you my order to have them removed so that they wouldn't intimidate the Croats and the Muslims, then they were moved out of the settlement. Still they continued doing things that were wrong. Then another order of mine was issued that Defence have in their possession, it's an original, for them to be driven out of Herzegovina. I risked my own head because we had them removed. As for the destruction of the mosques, well things were being destroyed all over. It was based on the principle of: If you destroy mine, I'll destroy something of yours, but it was not organised. No command had anything to do with it. It was simply that one morning a religious building would show -- would be destroyed. The Catholic cathedral in the centre of Trebinje next to the market-place was left untouched when the Dayton Accords were put in place. Why? Because the Orthodox church in Dubrovnik had not been destroyed. If it had been, no God would have saved the cathedral in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you were shown part of your interview from "Free Europe" or something which is P6625 [as interpreted], page 3. There there is some reference to a message of Allah, and you said that Allah told them to leave Trebinje, and you told Mr. Tieger that it was a fabrication and that it cannot be found in the SDA documents. Can we actually find it in their documents?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely, Mr. President. I am no man of lies. Whatever I say is something I stand by. I not only say things but I can prove things with documents, persuasive documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D7093, the first two pages of this document were admitted as D something, but we have to offer this number. It was shown by the Prosecution. In the first version the third page was not admitted, so can we first go to the first page and then to the third page. 1D7093.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown this document today, were you not. Actually, this order or this instruction was quoted to you, instructions for moving out of Trebinje by Mr. Hasan Cengic; correct? The 20th of January, 1993, is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The answer was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the fourth page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now would you please look at page 3, the Municipal Board of the SDA in Trebinje where it says: "Acting on the instructions of the headquarters ..." and so on and so forth, "I'm inviting you to do the following." It says here the universal principles of the Islamic faith, the Serbo-Chetnik armada, that will be us I suppose, and then somewhere in the middle of the page it says: "We appeal to you to quietly and cautiously and bravely and in an organised manner begin leaving temporarily our beloved Trebinje which will always be a Muslim Bosnian Trebinje to which we will return in triumph with the help of Allah and the forces of our state of Bosnia and Herzegovina." How did you interpret this? Who was it who put pressure on people by quoting Allah? Who was it who was trying to persuade Muslims to leave?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Every question is for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I spoke to a Muslim before their exodus started in groups. There had been smaller groups, Muslims, who were moving out, but at the same time 6.000 Serbs fled Trebinje trying to escape war, trying to save their lives. That person invited me to come and talk to him not in his house but in the wood. He told me that he was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDA and he said: You told us in the municipality that it was the black devil who was chasing us away from Cetin [phoen]. He took out some papers and told me: I'm going to give you these but I need you to give me guarantees for a safe life in Trebinje. I couldn't do that. I myself was shot at, my cousin was killed by the Serbian army, so I told him there are no guarantees. A lot of refugees came, a lot of bereaved people, there's no control, people are armed, the state is in a state of disrepair, who could control all that? The second solution was for me to get papers for me and my son to move abroad and for my family to move to Serbia. He received all the necessary papers and the Muslim who was a member of the Municipal Board gave me these two papers, one from Hasan Cengic and their president and there are no forgeries there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll up a little and can we see page 2 in English where it says: "We assure you that this is not a road to uncertainty and a road to peril. What is waiting for us there are reception centres," and so on and so forth. "We will be distributed." What was the purpose of this order for people to leave Trebinje en masse? What was the goal of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there was just one goal. First of all, the Croatian flag and the Muslim flag were tied together. The Yugoslav People's Army had left and they were purported to be the guarantor of peace, and all of a sudden there was a conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO on the one side with us on the other side, and in our unit we had 12 Muslims. Obviously Alija Izetbegovic was bothered by that. The fact that their own men were fighting against Muslims, and it was not just Alija who was bothered by that. That's one thing. The second thing is that of course our international negotiations were being undermined, the negotiations in Geneva, that is, and that was one of the main objectives because as you know Mr. Izetbegovic said: "I will sacrifice peace in order to gain a sovereign Bosnia." Why is that? Muslims did not want to stay in Yugoslavia because they would have been a minority there, and we could not accept to remain living in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a minority. So that made a conflict inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you understand the investigation of the international organisation which toured reception centres in Montenegro? What came out of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a caution -- well, let's monitor the response in light of how we approached this matter earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Karadzic follows. If Mr. Robinson could advise the accused. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't -- Excellency, I didn't mention the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. I wasn't and I wasn't suggesting that Mr. Karadzic had breached any kind of confidentiality. But simply now that we're moving into this, there's very -- it's very ripe for the possibility of the witness doing so inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will leave that. If you do not know anything for a fact I'll leave it. Can we go back to the previous page. On line 10 on the previous page you said that you had 12 Muslims in the Trebinje brigade. How many Muslims were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: 412, Mr. President. I suppose that they didn't hear me well. 412 Muslims in just one war brigade in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to page 1 in this document, the first -- the very first page. Let us look at this page, paragraph 2, where it says: "Sell some of the movable and immovable property or, if possible, leave it in the custody of reliable Serbs..." Did this really materialise?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To a large extent, yes. Those Muslims who had close friends among the Serbs entrusted them with their houses and that's how Trebinje was preserved. Not a single house was destroyed and there is a document issued by the international commissariat for refugees. When they arrived I got a letter of commendation for having been able to preserve all the Muslim property. Nothing was torched, nothing was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now we will ask you to send us that and we will bar table it. Why did this Muslim ask you to meet in a wood, not in a house or in an apartment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I thought that he was just provoking me. He called me during the night and we agreed that he -- that he would arrive at my office the following day at 7.00 in the morning but he didn't. And then he again called me the following night and I told him you are a Muslim and you're probably provoking me. The answer was no. He said I came close to the municipality. I was afraid if my people saw me entering your office that wouldn't be good. We met very close to the city. There was another person with him. I did him a favour like I did to all the others and that's when he handed me over the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at paragraph 3 where it says: "Do not refrain from putting pressure or even force against those Muslims who do not act according to this order." Who would it have been to put pressure and what has this paragraph got to do with his request to meet in the wood?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, he did -- would not -- didn't want to hand this over to me so that they could learn. I'm -- still don't want to say his name. I don't know what pressures would have taken place, what were the modalities that were designed. I don't know. In any case, they threatened their own people by force in order to make them leave Trebinje. Where it says here that it was on the 12th of December and then on the 30th of December, only six days later I spent the entire day writing those passes. Entire families came so we issued passes to the families and then to the individuals if the individuals came, and then if possible I would like to tell the following thing to this Trial Chamber: When they asked for buses, I ordered that two Trebinje companies prepared their buses, to have a police escorts, and before that the canyon of the river Trebisnjica had to be secured in order to prevent any crimes from happening, gentlemen. And then they left en masse. They did not need any passes. They were escorted by the police all the way to Montenegro, to their destination there. And there were no interviews of the kind that we heard about the interviews that were purportedly published in newspapers. This is all fabrication, the things that we heard from the Prosecutor. There were no interviews given on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that the dates are wrong. Instead of 12th December it should be 20 January.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So instead of December it has to be 20 December and -- 20 January and 30 January?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent the entire day writing those passes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Too fast, too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far is Montenegro from you? Which is a majority population there, and who was the president of Montenegro at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The border of Montenegro is near Trebinje. When it comes to the border between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is between the municipalities of Niksic and Trebinje. From the centre of Trebinje to Montenegro there is about 20 kilometres. The president of Montenegro at the time was Mr. Momir Bulatovic and the president of the government or prime minister was Milo Djukanovic. The majority population there are Serbs, but they travelled in the direction of Osinja [phoen] where there are municipalities with predominantly Muslim population. They spent very little time. Everything had been organised. Most of them went to Denmark. Some of them went to Turkey. Very few of them went elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now tell me at that time was Montenegro independent? What state was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation, or rather, it was a Rump Yugoslavia, Mr. President. It was a state of Montenegro and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger mentioned that you had been charged with the events in Ravno. Can you tell the Trial Chamber when did the fighting around Ravno take place? Who was in charge? Were you ever convicted for that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just recently the second OG arrived. A lot of troops and a lot of equipment arrived over night. They were not billeted in the barracks which were in a good state of repairs and rather empty. They were billeted in a modern pensioners' home. It was still not in use but it was very well equipped. On the following morning when the director of that retirement home which was still not in use came to me to complain about the arrival of the troops, I drafted a request to them to move to the barracks. You received that request together with the rest of the material. Two high-ranked officers came to see me. They enjoyed all the privileges in the former state and they asked me who wrote this. I said I did, and I told them read this and don't risk being arrested during the day. And I was reading, again the document is with your team. It says here: "Mr. Vucurevic, we are very sorry that you do not understand that the Yugoslav People's Army has been de-politicised and that you do not have to interfere with these matters. You should read the order of the federal secretary for national defence, the army General Veljko Kadijevic, and then you will understand everything." Under paragraph 3 it says that: "There is a ban on any sort of politicisation, that civilians must not come to the command post, that they must not mingle with the troops, and if any such thing would happen they should urgently be arrested and handed over to military courts." I'm sure that you have the original of that order because I gave it to you, so I really could not go there, let alone try and turn their barrels in the direction I wanted to. For them we were a transitional measure from one day to the next. They did not trust us. They were communist. Yugoslav People's Army conflicted with the Croatian paramilitaries on the 1st of October, 1991. That was at Ivanica in the municipality of Trebinje which was my municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska and when the Croatian paramilitaries killed 11 soldiers while they were having their breakfast, and then on the following day they killed another seven, a total of 18. That was not a Serbo-Chetnik army. Gentlemen, there was one Croat, one Muslim, four Albanians among those who were killed among the troops. What I'm saying here is that they were members of the army from the then four republics and four peoples of the former Yugoslavia, and then the army decided to retaliate. The municipality of Ravno suffered a lot, but that was all far from us. We did not interfere in any way. Even if we had wanted to intervene we couldn't. We didn't dare do anything. So any interference with the matters of the command and the matters of the army when it came to the civilian personnel, that was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 27 it is stated that in 2004 you were removed from the position as the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party by the international commissioner. Can you tell us whether you were the only one to whom that happened? Were you removed because of something that had happened during the war or was there allegations against you about things that were happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: It was neither nor. At that time the Serbian Democratic Party suffered blows from outside and from the inside, and then the high commissioner inappropriately removed from the Main Board a total of 58 of us all by issuing one document. I apologise for counting myself among those most respectable members of the Serbian Democratic Party which suffered greatly as a result of that. That was a huge blow against the party, not against Bozidar Vucurevic or any other individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the main objections against those members of the Serbian Democratic Party? Did it have anything to do with me?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was written there that the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accord, and there were lots of stories to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, did the two of us meet after 1996 when his holiness Vasilije came? Did we ever meet again?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank God, since the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucurevic, for everything, for your testimony, for your co-operation, and for protecting your Muslim neighbours. We are proud of you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to say this. Ever since the JNA had left and since we were unprepared and laid our hopes in this unfortunate army, on the 18th of May, 1992, we had our border towards Croatia opened. Overnight the regular Croatian army, because in the meantime Croatia was recognised, occupied 78 villages in my municipality and burned 788 houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, that's not necessary. Mr. Vucurevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's unnecessary, Mr. Vucurevic. It's for the -- Mr. Karadzic to put questions if necessary. With respect to the last document, Mr. Karadzic, you referred to earlier to Exhibit D471. In the meantime I compared that with this one, 1D7093, and found that the current one has three pages. The previous one does not have the third page which is titled -- entitled as "Appeal." So would you like to tender this document separately or would you like to replace it? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we could just tender the third page of 1D7093 as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I need confirmation whether the two documents are identical, first two pages, because English translation looked a bit different each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, maybe we should admit the whole three pages then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that keeps -- may even keep the record a little bit straighter given the fact that they were -- these were admitted on two separate occasions, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit the last document as next D exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vucurevic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, the Chamber is minded to adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I didn't understand well. Do you need me tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.53 p.m.,
